bioghist.head: Black Panther Party and the New Haven trial
bioghist.p: The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense (BPP) was a Black revolutionary party founded in 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland, California. The group was founded to protect members of African American communities from police brutality and was heavily inspired by the ideologies of Black nationalism, socialism, and armed self-defense. It also became a target of J. Edgar Hoover, director of the FBI, an opponent of communist subversive groups. Newton and Seale started BPP in response to the continued violence Black communities faced opting away from the nonviolent movements and integrationalist goals of the Civil Rights Movement led by Martin Luther King Jr. BPP used direct action to aid Black communities through Survival Programs that fed children, registered communities to vote, and offered free healthcare.

In 1969, Alex Rackley, a member of the New Haven chapter of the Panthers, was abducted, tortured and killed by fellow members who suspected he was a police informant. Nine defendants, the "New Haven Nine," were indicted on charges related to the case, including Booby Seale, Ericka Huggins, Warren Kimbro, George Sams, Jr., and Lonnie McLucas. Sams declared that Bobby Seale, who had been speaking at Yale University during the time Rackley was held prisoner, had directly ordered the murder. As jury selection for the trials began in May 1970, thousands of Black Panther supporters arrived for a May Day rally in New Haven, where organizers were urging violent action. Fears of rioting led to the stationing of National Guard units around the city and the temporary closure of many local businesses. The six-month trial ended with a hung jury for Bobby Seale and Ericka Huggins after which charges were dropped. George Sams and Warren Kimbro were charged with Rackley's murder and Lonnie McLucas was charged with conspiracy to commit murder.

relatedmaterial.head: Related Materials
relatedmaterial.p: Related materials: Black Panther Party collection (GEN MSS 2097); Catherine Roraback Collection of Ericka Huggins Papers (JWJ MSS 96); Thomas Strong photographs of New Haven May Day rally (MS 2030); May Day Rally and Yale collection (RU 86); and Robert Templeton drawings and sketches related to the trial of Bobby G. Seale and Ericka Huggins, New Haven, Connecticut (JWJ MSS 33).

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Materials in the Black Panther Trial records document the activities of David Rosen during the New Haven Black Panther trials. The majority of the records contain David Rosen's legal files related to Bobby Seale's trial. There is also material related to Ericka Huggins, Seale's co-defendant and the trials of other Black Panther members in different jurisdictions. The records include memoranda, motions, statements, police reports, exhibit documents, pressm and research generated for the trial.
